newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens Q1 profit down, but forecast intact.
newsitem.headline: Siemens Q1 profit down, but forecast intact.

text.p: German engineering giant Siemens AG said on Tuesday that group net profits fell slightly in the first quarter of its 1996/97 business year, but added a forecast of unchanged full-year profits was still intact.
The company said that group net profits fell in the first quarter, ending December 31, to 478 million marks ($289.5 million) from 503 million marks in the same period a year earlier.
"The numbers are in line with the forecast," a Siemens spokesman told Reuters.
Group net profits rose last year to 3.3 billion marks from 1.9 billion marks.
Siemens said the fall in first quarter net income resulted from falling semiconductor prices.
Group sales rose in the first quarter to 20.9 billion marks from 19.7 billion. Incoming orders were up sharply to 27 billion from 22.2 billion marks.
The concern's workforce fell to 377,000 at the end of 1996, down slightly from the end-September figure of 379,000, with some jobs being cut in Germany and added abroad.
Siemens said in a statement that the pickup in new orders was largely due to major projects, with growth led by energy, transport, communications and information operations.
Foreign orders led the way, rising by 130 percent in the Asia-Pacific region and by 37 percent in the Americas. Orders were up by eight percent in Germany.
Around two percentage points of Siemens' international growth can be attributed to the impact of the strong dollar. But the company said it expected growth to level off.
"Following the amassing of major projects in the first quarter, growth is expected to normalise for the remainder of the year," the company said.
Sales, up six percent in the first quarter, grew evenly both at home and abroad, with the group's power, energy, communications and information divisions posting double-digit rates.

The industry division, however saw sales decline due mainly to weak demand for capital goods in Germany's construction sector. Semiconductors was hit by sharp price erosion, primarily for memory chips.
